q: Who created us?
a: God created us.

q: Who is God?
a: God is the most perfect Being, Creator and Lord of heaven and earth.

q: What does "most perfect" mean?
a: "Most perfect" means that in God there is every perfection, without defect and without limit; that is, He is infinite power, wisdom, and goodness.

q: What does "Creator" mean?
a: "Creator" means that God made all things from nothing.

q: What does "Lord" mean?
a: "Lord" means that God is the absolute master of all things.

q: Does God have a body as we do?
a: God has no body, but is most pure spirit.

q: Where is God?
a: God is in heaven, on earth, and in every place: He is the Immense.

q: Has God always existed?
a: God has always existed and will always exist: He is the Eternal.

q: Does God know all things?
a: God knows all things, even our thoughts: He is the All-Knowing.

q: Can God do all things?
a: God can do all that He wills: He is the Almighty.

q: Can God also do evil?
a: God cannot do evil, because He cannot will it, being infinite goodness; but He tolerates it in order to leave creatures free, knowing how to draw good even from evil.

q: Does God care for created things?
a: God cares for and provides for created things, and He preserves and directs them all to their proper end with infinite wisdom, goodness, and justice.

q: For what end did God create us?
a: God created us to know Him, love Him, and serve Him in this life, and afterward to enjoy Him in the next, in heaven.

q: What is heaven?
a: Heaven is the eternal enjoyment of God, our happiness, and, in Him, of every other good, without any evil.

q: Who deserves heaven?
a: He deserves heaven who is good, that is, who loves and faithfully serves God, and dies in His grace.

q: What do the wicked deserve, who do not serve God and die in mortal sin?
a: The wicked, who do not serve God and die in mortal sin, deserve hell.

q: What is hell?
a: Hell is the eternal suffering of the privation of God, our happiness, and of fire, with every other evil and without any good.

q: Why does God reward the good and punish the wicked?
a: God rewards the good and punishes the wicked because He is infinite justice.

q: Is there only one God?
a: There is only one God, but in three Persons equal and distinct, who are the Most Holy Trinity.

q: What are the names of the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity are called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

q: Of the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity, has any one been incarnate and made man?
a: Of the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity, the second, that is, the Son, was incarnate and made man.

q: What is the name of the Son of God made man?
a: The Son of God made man is called Jesus Christ.

q: Who is Jesus Christ?
a: Jesus Christ is the second Person of the Most Holy Trinity, that is, the Son of God made man.

q: Is Jesus Christ God and man?
a: Yes, Jesus Christ is true God and true man.

q: Why did the Son of God become man?
a: The Son of God became man to save us, that is, to redeem us from sin and to win heaven back for us.

q: What did Jesus Christ do to save us?
a: To save us, Jesus Christ made satisfaction for our sins by suffering and sacrificing Himself on the Cross, and He taught us to live according to God.

q: To live according to God, what must we do?
a: To live according to God, we must BELIEVE THE TRUTHS REVEALED by Him and KEEP HIS COMMANDMENTS, with the help of His GRACE, which is obtained through THE SACRAMENTS and PRAYER.

q: What are the truths revealed by God?
a: The truths revealed by God are chiefly those summarized in the Creed, or Apostles' Creed, and they are called truths of faith because we must believe them with full faith as taught by God, who neither deceives nor can be deceived.

q: What is the "Creed" or "Apostles' Creed"?
a: The Creed, or Apostles' Creed, is a profession of the principal mysteries and of other truths revealed by God through Jesus Christ and the Apostles, and taught by the Church.

q: What is a mystery?
a: A mystery is a truth above, but not contrary to, reason, which we believe because God has revealed it.

q: What are the principal mysteries of the Faith professed in the Creed?
a: The principal mysteries of the Faith professed in the Creed are two: the Unity and Trinity of God; the Incarnation, Passion, and Death of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

q: Do we profess and express the two principal mysteries of the Faith also in another way?
a: We also profess and express the two principal mysteries of the Faith by the Sign of the Cross, which for this reason is the sign of the Christian.

q: How is the Sign of the Cross made?
a: The Sign of the Cross is made by raising the right hand to the forehead, saying: In the name of the Father; then to the breast, saying: and of the Son; then to the left shoulder and to the right, saying: and of the Holy Spirit; and ending with the word Amen.

q: In the Sign of the Cross, how do we express the two principal mysteries of the Faith?
a: In the Sign of the Cross, by the words we express the Unity and Trinity of God, and by the figure of the cross we express the Passion and Death of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

q: Is it useful to make the Sign of the Cross?
a: It is most useful to make the Sign of the Cross often and devoutly, because it is an outward act of faith that revives this virtue in us, overcomes human respect and temptations, and obtains for us graces from God.

q: When is it good to make the Sign of the Cross?
a: It is always good to make the Sign of the Cross, but especially before and after every act of religion, before and after meals and rest, and in dangers of soul and body.

q: What does "Unity of God" mean?
a: "Unity of God" means that there is only one God.

q: What does "Trinity of God" mean?
a: "Trinity of God" means that in God there are three equal Persons, really distinct: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

q: What does "three really distinct Persons" mean?
a: "Three really distinct Persons" means that in God one Person is not the other, although all three are one and the same God.

q: Do we understand how the three divine Persons, though really distinct, are one God?
a: We do not understand, nor can we understand, how the three divine Persons, though really distinct, are one God: it is a mystery.

q: Who is the first Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The first Person of the Most Holy Trinity is the Father.

q: Who is the second Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The second Person of the Most Holy Trinity is the Son.

q: Who is the third Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The third Person of the Most Holy Trinity is the Holy Spirit.

q: Why is the Father the first Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The Father is the first Person of the Most Holy Trinity because He does not proceed from any other Person, and from Him proceed the other two, that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

q: Why is the Son the second Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The Son is the second Person of the Most Holy Trinity because He is begotten of the Father, and is, together with the Father, the principle of the Holy Spirit.

q: Why is the Holy Spirit the third Person of the Most Holy Trinity?
a: The Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Most Holy Trinity because He proceeds from the Father and the Son.

q: Is each Person of the Most Holy Trinity God?
a: Yes, each Person of the Most Holy Trinity is God.

q: If each divine Person is God, are the three divine Persons therefore three Gods?
a: The three divine Persons are not three Gods, but only one God, because they have the same one divine nature or substance.

q: Are the three divine Persons equal, or is one of them greater, more powerful, and more wise?
a: Since the three divine Persons are one God, they are equal in all things, and they have every perfection and every operation equally in common; although certain perfections and the corresponding works are attributed more to one Person than to another, as power and creation are to the Father.

q: Was the Father at least before the Son and the Holy Spirit?
a: The Father was not before the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the three divine Persons, having in common the one divine nature, which is eternal, are equally eternal.

q: Why is God called "Creator of heaven and earth"?
a: God is called Creator of heaven and earth, that is, of the world, because He made it from nothing, and to make from nothing is to create.

q: Is the whole world the work of God?
a: The whole world is the work of God; and in its greatness, beauty, and wonderful order it shows us His infinite power, wisdom, and goodness.

q: Did God create only what is material in the world?
a: God did not create only what is material in the world, but also pure spirits; and He creates the soul of every man.

q: Who are the pure spirits?
a: Pure spirits are intelligent beings without bodies.

q: How do we know that created pure spirits exist?
a: We know that created pure spirits exist from Faith.

q: Which created pure spirits does Faith make known to us?
a: Faith makes known to us the good pure spirits, that is, the Angels, and the wicked ones, that is, the demons.

q: Who are the Angels?
a: The Angels are the invisible ministers of God, and also our Guardians, since God has entrusted each man to one of them.

q: Have we any duties toward the Angels?
a: Toward the Angels we have the duty of veneration; and toward our Guardian Angel we have also the duty of being grateful, of listening to his inspirations, and of never offending his presence by sin.

q: Who are the demons?
a: The demons are angels who rebelled against God through pride and were cast down into hell, and who, out of hatred for God, tempt man to evil.

q: Who is man?
a: Man is a rational being, composed of soul and body.

q: What is the soul?
a: The soul is the spiritual part of man, by which he lives, understands, and is free, and therefore capable of knowing, loving, and serving God.

q: Does the soul of man die with the body?
a: The soul of man does not die with the body, but lives forever, since it is spiritual.

q: What care must we have of the soul?
a: We must have the greatest care of the soul, because it is the better and immortal part of us, and only by saving the soul shall we be eternally happy.

q: In what way is man free?
a: Man is free in that he can do a thing or not do it, or do one thing rather than another, as we plainly feel within ourselves.

q: If man is free, can he also do evil?
a: Man can — that is, is able — to do evil also; but he must not do it, precisely because it is evil; freedom must be used only for good.

q: Who were the first human beings?
a: The first human beings were Adam and Eve, created immediately by God; all others descend from them, and for this reason they are called the progenitors of mankind.

q: Was man created weak and miserable as we now are?
a: Man was not created weak and miserable as we now are, but in a happy state, with a destiny and gifts above human nature.

q: What destiny did man receive from God?
a: Man received from God the most exalted destiny of seeing and enjoying Him eternally — the infinite Good — and because this is wholly above the capacity of nature, he received together with it, in order to attain it, a supernatural power which is called grace.

q: Besides grace, what else had God given to man?
a: Besides grace, God had given man exemption from the weaknesses and miseries of life and from the necessity of dying, provided he had not sinned, as Adam, the head of mankind, unfortunately did by tasting the forbidden fruit.

q: What kind of sin was Adam's?
a: Adam's sin was a grave sin of pride and disobedience.

q: What harm did Adam's sin cause?
a: Adam's sin stripped him and all men of grace and of every other supernatural gift, making them subject to sin, to the devil, to death, to ignorance, to evil inclinations, and to every other misery, and excluding them from heaven.

q: What is the sin called to which Adam subjected mankind by his fault?
a: The sin to which Adam subjected mankind by his fault is called original, because, having been committed at the beginning of mankind, it is transmitted with our nature to all human beings at their origin.

q: In what does original sin consist?
a: Original sin consists in the privation of original grace, which by God's disposition we ought to have but do not have, because the head of mankind, by his disobedience, deprived himself and all of us, his descendants, of it.

q: How is original sin "voluntary," and therefore a fault for us?
a: Original sin is voluntary and therefore a fault for us only because Adam, as the head of mankind, voluntarily committed it; and for this reason God does not punish, but simply does not reward with heaven, one who has only original sin.

q: Was man, because of original sin, to remain forever excluded from heaven?
a: Man, because of original sin, would have remained forever excluded from heaven, had not God, to save him, promised and sent from heaven His own Son, that is, Jesus Christ.

q: In what way did the Son of God become man?
a: The Son of God became man by taking a body and a soul, as we have, in the most pure womb of the Virgin Mary, by the work of the Holy Spirit.

q: In becoming man, did the Son of God cease to be God?
a: The Son of God, in becoming man, did not cease to be God, but, remaining true God, began to be also true man.

q: Are there two natures in Jesus Christ?
a: In Jesus Christ there are two natures: the divine nature and the human nature.

q: Are there in Jesus Christ also two persons together with the two natures?
a: In Jesus Christ, with the two natures, there are not two persons, but only one — the divine Person of the Son of God.

q: How was Jesus Christ known to be the Son of God?
a: Jesus Christ was known to be the Son of God because God the Father proclaimed Him such at the Baptism and at the Transfiguration, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. III. 17; Luke IX. 35); and because Jesus Himself declared the same in His earthly life.

q: Did Jesus Christ always exist?
a: Jesus Christ as God always existed; as man He began to be from the moment of the Incarnation.

q: From whom was Jesus Christ born?
a: Jesus Christ was born of Mary ever Virgin, who is therefore called and truly is the Mother of God.

q: Was Saint Joseph not the father of Jesus Christ?
a: Saint Joseph was not the true father of Jesus Christ, but His foster-father; that is, as the spouse of Mary and the guardian of Jesus, he was believed to be His father without actually being so.

q: Where was Jesus Christ born?
a: Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem, in a stable, and was laid in a manger.

q: Why did Jesus Christ wish to be poor?
a: Jesus Christ wished to be poor in order to teach us to be humble and not to place our happiness in the riches, honors, and pleasures of the world.

q: What did Jesus Christ do in His earthly life?
a: Jesus Christ, in His earthly life, taught us by example and by word to live according to God, and confirmed His doctrine by miracles; finally, to blot out sin, reconcile us with God, and reopen heaven for us, He offered Himself in sacrifice on the Cross, "the one Mediator between God and men."

q: What is a miracle?
a: A miracle is a perceptible event, above all the forces and laws of nature, and therefore such that it can come only from God, the Master of nature.

q: By what miracles especially did Jesus Christ confirm His doctrine and prove that He is true God?
a: Jesus Christ confirmed His doctrine and proved that He is true God especially by restoring in an instant sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, health to every kind of sick person, and life to the dead; by commanding as Master over demons and the forces of nature; and above all by His Resurrection from death.

q: Did Jesus Christ die as God or as man?
a: Jesus Christ died as man, because as God He could neither suffer nor die.

q: What became of Jesus Christ after His death?
a: After His death, Jesus Christ descended in soul to Limbo, to the souls of the just who had died until then, to lead them with Him into heaven; then He rose, taking again His body which had been buried.

q: How long did the body of Jesus Christ remain in the tomb?
a: The body of Jesus Christ remained in the tomb three days, not whole, from the evening of Friday until the dawn of the day now called Easter Sunday.

q: What did Jesus Christ do after His resurrection?
a: Jesus Christ, after His resurrection, remained on earth forty days; then He ascended into heaven, where He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.

q: Why did Jesus Christ remain on earth forty days after His resurrection?
a: Jesus Christ remained on earth forty days after His resurrection in order to show that He had truly risen, to confirm His disciples in their faith in Him, and to instruct them more deeply in His doctrine.

q: Is Jesus Christ now only in heaven?
a: Jesus Christ is not now only in heaven, but as God He is in every place, and as God and man He is in heaven and in the Most Holy Sacrament of the altar.

q: Will Jesus Christ ever again return visibly to this earth?
a: Jesus Christ will return visibly to this earth at the end of the world to judge the living and the dead, that is, all men, both good and wicked.

q: Will Jesus Christ wait until the end of the world to judge us?
a: Jesus Christ will not wait until the end of the world to judge us, but will judge each one immediately after death.

q: Are there two judgments?
a: There are two judgments: one particular, of each soul, immediately after death; the other universal, of all men, at the end of the world.

q: On what will Jesus Christ judge us?
a: Jesus Christ will judge us on the good and the evil done in life, even on our thoughts and our omissions.

q: After the particular judgment, what becomes of the soul?
a: After the particular judgment, the soul, if it is without sin and without debt of punishment, goes to heaven; if it has some venial sin or some debt of punishment, it goes to purgatory until it has made satisfaction; if it is in mortal sin, then, as a rebel beyond conversion to God, it goes to hell.

q: Where do children who die without Baptism go?
a: Children who die without Baptism go to Limbo, where there is no supernatural reward nor any pain; because, having only original sin and nothing more, they do not merit heaven, but neither do they merit hell or purgatory.

q: What is purgatory?
a: Purgatory is the temporary suffering of the privation of God, and of other pains which take away from the soul every remnant of sin in order to render it worthy to see God.

q: Can we help and even free the souls from the pains of purgatory?
a: We can help and even free the souls from the pains of purgatory by suffrages, that is, by prayers, indulgences, almsgiving, and other good works, and above all by the Holy Mass.

q: Is it certain that heaven and hell exist?
a: It is certain that heaven and hell exist: God has revealed it, often promising to the good eternal life and His own joy, and threatening the wicked with perdition and eternal fire.

q: How long will heaven and hell last?
a: Heaven and hell will last eternally.

q: What is the Church?
a: The Church is the society of true Christians, that is, of the baptized who profess the faith and doctrine of Jesus Christ, share in His sacraments, and obey the Pastors established by Him.

q: By whom was the Church founded?
a: The Church was founded by Jesus Christ, who gathered His faithful into a society, placed it under the Apostles with Saint Peter as its head, and gave it the sacrifice, the sacraments, and the Holy Spirit who gives it life.

q: Which is the Church of Jesus Christ?
a: The Church of Jesus Christ is the Roman Catholic Church, because she alone is one, holy, catholic, and apostolic, as He willed her to be.

q: Why is the Church one?
a: The Church is one because all her members had, have, and will always have one and the same faith, sacrifice, sacraments, and visible head, the Roman Pontiff, successor of Saint Peter, thus all forming one body, the Mystical Body of Jesus Christ.

q: Why is the Church holy?
a: The Church is holy because Jesus Christ, her invisible head, and the Spirit who gives her life are holy; because the doctrine, the sacrifice, and the sacraments in her are holy, and all her members are called to sanctify themselves; and because many have indeed been, are, and will be saints.

q: Why is the Church catholic?
a: The Church is catholic, that is, universal, because she is established and adapted for all human beings and is spread throughout the whole earth.

q: Why is the Church apostolic?
a: The Church is apostolic because she is founded upon the Apostles and their preaching, and is governed by their successors, the legitimate Pastors, who without interruption and without alteration continue to transmit both her doctrine and her authority.

q: Who are the legitimate Pastors of the Church?
a: The legitimate Pastors of the Church are the Pope, or Supreme Pontiff, and the Bishops united with him.

q: Who is the Pope?
a: The Pope is the successor of Saint Peter in the See of Rome and in the primacy, that is, in the universal apostolate and episcopate; and therefore the visible head, Vicar of Jesus Christ the invisible head, of the whole Church, which for this reason is called Roman Catholic.

q: What do the Pope and the Bishops united with him constitute?
a: The Pope and the Bishops united with him constitute the teaching Church, so called because she has from Jesus Christ the mission to teach the divine truths and laws to all human beings, who from her alone receive the full and certain knowledge of them that is necessary to live as Christians.

q: Can the teaching Church err in teaching us the truths revealed by God?
a: The teaching Church cannot err in teaching us the truths revealed by God: she is infallible, because, as Jesus Christ promised, "the Spirit of truth" (John XV. 26) assists her continually.

q: Can the Pope, by himself, err in teaching us the truths revealed by God?
a: The Pope, by himself, cannot err in teaching us the truths revealed by God; that is, he is infallible like the Church when, as Pastor and Teacher of all Christians, he defines doctrines concerning faith and morals.

q: Can any Church outside the Roman Catholic Church be the Church of Jesus Christ, or at least a part of it?
a: No Church outside the Roman Catholic Church can be the Church of Jesus Christ, or a part of it, because no other Church can possess together with her those singular distinctive marks — one, holy, catholic, and apostolic — as in fact none of the other Churches calling themselves Christian possesses them.

q: Why did Jesus Christ institute the Church?
a: Jesus Christ instituted the Church so that human beings might find in her a sure guide and the means of holiness and of eternal salvation.

q: What are the means of holiness and of eternal salvation found in the Church?
a: The means of holiness and of eternal salvation found in the Church are the true faith, the sacrifice and the sacraments, and the mutual spiritual helps such as prayer, counsel, and example.

q: Are the means of holiness and of eternal salvation common to all human beings?
a: The means of holiness and of eternal salvation are common to all who belong to the Church, that is, to the faithful, who in the apostolic writings are called saints; therefore their union and their sharing in those means is the communion of saints in holy things.

q: Why are the faithful in the Church called saints?
a: The faithful in the Church are called saints because they are consecrated to God, justified or sanctified by the sacraments, and bound to live as saints.

q: What does "communion of saints" mean?
a: "Communion of saints" means that all the faithful, forming one body in Jesus Christ, share in all the good that is and is done in that body, that is, in the universal Church, provided they are not impeded by attachment to sin.

q: Are the blessed in heaven and the souls in purgatory in the communion of saints?
a: The blessed in heaven and the souls in purgatory are also in the communion of saints, because, joined to one another and to us by charity, they receive — the former our prayers, the latter our suffrages — and they all repay us with their intercession before God.

q: Who is outside the communion of saints?
a: Outside the communion of saints is whoever is outside the Church, that is, the damned, unbelievers, Jews, heretics, apostates, schismatics, and excommunicates.

q: Who are the unbelievers?
a: The unbelievers are the unbaptized who in no way believe in the promised Savior, that is, in the Messiah or Christ, such as idolaters and Muslims.

q: Who are the Jews?
a: The Jews are the unbaptized who profess the law of Moses and do not believe that Jesus is the promised Messiah or Christ.

q: Who are the heretics?
a: The heretics are the baptized who obstinately refuse to believe some truth revealed by God and taught by the Church — for example, the Protestants.

q: Who are the apostates?
a: The apostates are the baptized who, by an outward act, renounce the Catholic faith they had previously professed.

q: Who are the schismatics?
a: The schismatics are the baptized who obstinately refuse to submit to the legitimate Pastors, and are therefore separated from the Church, even if they do not deny any truth of faith.

q: Who are the excommunicates?
a: The excommunicates are the baptized who have been excluded, on account of very grave faults, from the communion of the Church, so that they may not pervert others and may be punished and corrected by this extreme remedy.

q: Is it a serious harm to be outside the Church?
a: To be outside the Church is a most serious harm, because outside her one has neither the established means of salvation nor the sure guide to eternal salvation, which is the only thing truly necessary for man.

q: Can one who is outside the Church be saved?
a: One who is outside the Church through his own fault and dies without perfect contrition is not saved; but one who finds himself outside her through no fault of his own and lives well can be saved through the love of charity, which unites him to God, and, in spirit, also to the Church, that is, to her soul.

q: What does "forgiveness of sins" mean?
a: "Forgiveness of sins" means that Jesus Christ has given to the Apostles and to their successors the power to forgive every sin in the Church.

q: How are sins forgiven in the Church?
a: In the Church sins are forgiven chiefly by the sacraments of Baptism and Penance, instituted by Jesus Christ for this purpose.

q: What is sin?
a: Sin is an offense against God by disobedience to His law.

q: How many kinds of sin are there?
a: There are two kinds of sin: original and actual.

q: What is original sin?
a: Original sin is the sin that mankind committed in Adam, its head, and which from Adam every man contracts by natural descent.

q: Was anyone among the children of Adam ever preserved from original sin?
a: Among the children of Adam, only Mary Most Holy was preserved from original sin; for, having been chosen as Mother of God, she was "full of grace" (Luke I. 28), and therefore without sin from the very first instant; and for this reason the Church celebrates her Immaculate Conception.

q: How is original sin blotted out?
a: Original sin is blotted out by Holy Baptism.

q: What is actual sin?
a: Actual sin is the sin that is committed voluntarily by one who has the use of reason.

q: In how many ways is actual sin committed?
a: Actual sin is committed in four ways: in thoughts, in words, in deeds, and in omissions.

q: How many kinds of actual sin are there?
a: There are two kinds of actual sin: mortal and venial.

q: What is mortal sin?
a: Mortal sin is a disobedience to the law of God in a grave matter, committed with full advertence and deliberate consent.

q: Why is grave sin called mortal?
a: Grave sin is called mortal because it deprives the soul of divine grace, which is its life, takes from it its merits and its capacity to acquire new ones, and renders it deserving of eternal punishment, or eternal death, in hell.

q: If mortal sin renders man incapable of meriting, is it then useless for the sinner to do good works?
a: It is not useless for the sinner to do good works; on the contrary, he must do them, both so as not to grow worse by omitting them and falling into new sins, and so as in some way to dispose himself by them to conversion and to the recovery of God's grace.

q: How is the grace of God, lost through mortal sin, recovered?
a: The grace of God, lost through mortal sin, is recovered by a good sacramental confession or by perfect contrition, which frees one from sins, although the obligation of confessing them remains.

q: Together with grace, are the merits lost through mortal sin also recovered?
a: Together with grace, by God's supreme mercy, the merits lost through mortal sin are also recovered.

q: What is venial sin?
a: Venial sin is a disobedience to the law of God in a slight matter, or even in a matter grave in itself but without full advertence or consent.

q: Why is sin that is not grave called venial?
a: Sin that is not grave is called venial, that is, pardonable, because it does not take away grace, and pardon for it can be obtained by repentance and by good works, even without sacramental confession.

q: Is venial sin harmful to the soul?
a: Venial sin is harmful to the soul, because it cools its love for God, disposes it to mortal sin, and renders it deserving of temporal pains in this life and in the next.

q: Are all sins equal?
a: Sins are not all equal; and just as some venial sins are less light than others, so some mortal sins are graver and more deadly.

q: Among the mortal sins, which are graver and more deadly?
a: Among the mortal sins, the graver and more deadly are the sins against the Holy Spirit and those that cry to heaven for vengeance in the sight of God. 152 a. The Six Sins Against the Holy Spirit: 1. Despair of salvation; 2. Presumption of being saved without merit; 3. Impugning the known truth; 4. Envy of another's spiritual good; 5. Obstinacy in sin; 6. Final impenitence. 152 b. The Four Sins Crying to Heaven for Vengeance: 1. Wilful murder; 2. The sin of Sodom; 3. Oppression of the poor; 4. Defrauding labourers of their wages.

q: Why are the sins against the Holy Spirit among the graver and more deadly?
a: The sins against the Holy Spirit are among the graver and more deadly because by them man sets himself against the spiritual gifts of truth and of grace, and therefore, even when he is able to convert, he does so only with great difficulty.

q: Why are the sins that cry to heaven for vengeance in the sight of God among the graver and more deadly?
a: The sins that cry to heaven for vengeance in the sight of God are among the graver and more deadly because they are directly contrary to the good of mankind and most odious, so much so that they provoke God's chastisements more than other sins.

q: What is particularly helpful in keeping us far from sin?
a: What is particularly helpful in keeping us far from sin is the thought that God is everywhere and sees the secret of hearts, and the consideration of the Last Things, that is, of what awaits us at the end of this life and at the end of the world. 155 a. The Four Last Things: 1. Death; 2. Judgment; 3. Hell; 4. Heaven.

q: What awaits us at the end of this life?
a: At the end of this life, the pains and dissolution of death and the particular judgment await us.

q: What awaits us at the end of the world?
a: At the end of the world, the resurrection of the body and the universal judgment await us.

q: What does "resurrection of the body" mean?
a: "Resurrection of the body" means that our body, by the power of God, will be restored and reunited with the soul, in order to share, in eternal life, the reward or punishment it has merited.

q: What does "life everlasting" mean?
a: "Life everlasting" means that the reward, like the punishment, will last forever, and that the vision of God will be the true life and happiness of the soul, while the privation of Him will be the greatest unhappiness and, as it were, an eternal death.

q: What does the word "Amen" mean?
a: The word "Amen" means truly, so it is and so be it; and by it we confirm that all that we profess in the Creed is true, and we wish for ourselves the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection unto glory, and life everlasting in God.

q: What are the commandments of God?
a: The commandments of God, or Decalogue, are the moral laws that God in the Old Testament gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, and that Jesus Christ perfected in the New.

q: What does the Decalogue impose on us?
a: The Decalogue imposes on us the strictest natural duties toward God, ourselves, and our neighbor, as well as the other duties that flow from these — for example, those of one's state in life.

q: To what may our duties toward God and toward our neighbor be reduced?
a: Our duties toward God and toward our neighbor are reduced to charity, that is, to the "greatest and first commandment" of the love of God and to the "like" commandment of the love of neighbor: "On these two commandments," said Jesus Christ, "depend the whole Law and the Prophets" (Matt. XXII. 40). 163 a. The two commandments of charity: 1. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy soul, with all thy mind, and with all thy strength; 2. Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

q: Why is the commandment of the love of God the greatest commandment?
a: The commandment of the love of God is the greatest commandment because whoever observes it by loving God with all his soul certainly observes all the other commandments.

q: Can the commandments of God be observed?
a: The commandments of God can all be observed, and at all times, even in the strongest temptations, by the grace which God never denies to one who calls upon Him from the heart.

q: Are we bound to observe the commandments of God?
a: We are bound to observe the commandments of God because they are imposed by Him, our supreme Master, and are dictated by nature and by sound reason.

q: Does whoever transgresses the commandments of God sin gravely?
a: Whoever deliberately transgresses even one commandment of God in a grave matter sins gravely against God, and therefore deserves hell.

q: What must be noted in the commandments?
a: In the commandments we must note what is ordered and what is forbidden. § 2. The Commandments of God in Particular

q: What does the first commandment, "I am the Lord thy God: thou shalt not have other gods before me," order us?
a: The first commandment, "I am the Lord thy God: thou shalt not have other gods before me," orders us to be religious, that is, to believe in God and to love, adore, and serve Him as the one true God, Creator and Lord of all.

q: What does the first commandment forbid us?
a: The first commandment forbids us impiety, superstition, and irreligion; and also apostasy, heresy, voluntary doubt, and culpable ignorance of the truths of Faith.

q: What is impiety?
a: Impiety is the refusal to render any worship to God.

q: What is superstition?
a: Superstition is divine worship, or worship of latria, rendered to one who is not God, or to God Himself but in an unsuitable manner: such as idolatry, or the worship of false divinities and of creatures; recourse to the devil, to spirits, and to any suspect means in order to obtain things humanly impossible; the use of unsuitable, vain, or Church-forbidden rites.

q: What is irreligion?
a: Irreligion is irreverence toward God and toward divine things, such as tempting God, sacrilege or the profanation of a sacred person or thing, and simony, or the buying and selling of spiritual things or of things connected with the spiritual.

q: If the worship of creatures is superstition, how is the Catholic veneration of the Angels and of the Saints not superstition?
a: The Catholic veneration of the Angels and of the Saints is not superstition because it is not the divine worship, or worship of adoration, due to God alone: we do not adore them as God, but venerate them as the friends of God and for the gifts they have from Him; and thus, in honor of God Himself, who in the Angels and the Saints works wonders.

q: Who are the Saints?
a: The Saints are those who, by heroically practicing the virtues according to the teachings and examples of Jesus Christ, have merited a special glory in heaven and also on earth, where, by the authority of the Church, they are publicly honored and invoked.

q: Why do we venerate also the bodies of the Saints?
a: We also venerate the bodies of the Saints because they served them in the exercise of heroic virtues, were certainly temples of the Holy Spirit, and will rise glorious to eternal life.

q: Why do we venerate also the smallest relics and the images of the Saints?
a: We venerate also the smallest relics and the images of the Saints in their memory and honor, referring all veneration to them — wholly differently from the idolaters, who render to images or idols a divine worship.

q: Did not God in the Old Testament severely forbid images?
a: God in the Old Testament severely forbade images for adoration — and indeed nearly all images — as a proximate occasion of idolatry for the Hebrews, who lived among idolaters and were much inclined to superstition.

q: What does the second commandment, "Thou shalt not take the name of God in vain," forbid us?
a: The second commandment, "Thou shalt not take the name of God in vain," forbids us to dishonor God's name: therefore to name Him without respect; to blaspheme God, the Most Holy Virgin, the Saints, and holy things; and to make oaths that are false, unnecessary, or in any way unlawful.

q: What is an oath?
a: An oath is to call God to witness what one affirms or what one promises; therefore whoever swears to do evil, or perjures himself, gravely offends God, who is Holiness and Truth.

q: Is blasphemy a great sin?
a: Blasphemy is a great sin because it is an insult to and a mockery of God or His Saints, and often even a horrible heresy.

q: What does the second commandment order us?
a: The second commandment orders us always to have reverence for the holy name of God, and to fulfill our vows and our sworn promises.

q: What is a vow?
a: A vow is a promise made to God of some good that is pleasing to Him, to which we bind ourselves out of religion.

q: What does the third commandment, "Remember to keep holy the feast days," order us?
a: The third commandment, "Remember to keep holy the feast days," orders us to honor God on feast days with acts of outward worship, of which for Christians the essential is the Holy Mass.

q: Why must we perform acts of outward worship? Is it not enough to adore God, who is Spirit, inwardly in the heart?
a: It is not enough to adore God inwardly in the heart; we must also render Him the outward worship that is commanded, because we are subject to God in our whole being, soul and body, and we must give good example; and also because otherwise the religious spirit is lost.

q: What does the third commandment forbid us?
a: The third commandment forbids us, on feast days, servile works.

q: What works are called servile?
a: Servile works are the manual labors proper to artisans and workers.

q: Are all servile works forbidden on feast days?
a: On feast days are forbidden all servile works that are not necessary for life and for the service of God, and not justified by piety or by some other grave reason.

q: How is it fitting to occupy feast days?
a: It is fitting to occupy feast days for the good of the soul, by attending preaching and catechism and performing some good work, and also by resting the body, far from every vice and dissipation.

q: What does the fourth commandment, "Honor thy father and mother," order us?
a: The fourth commandment, "Honor thy father and mother," orders us to love, respect, and obey our parents and whoever has authority over us, that is, our superiors in authority.

q: What does the fourth commandment forbid us?
a: The fourth commandment forbids us to offend our parents and our superiors in authority, and to disobey them.

q: Why must we obey our superiors in authority?
a: We must obey our superiors in authority because "there is no authority except from God; ... therefore he who resists authority resists the ordinance of God" (Rom. XIII. 1-2).

q: What does the fifth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill," forbid us?
a: The fifth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill," forbids us to do harm to the life, both natural and spiritual, of our neighbor and of ourselves; and therefore it forbids us murder, suicide, dueling, woundings, blows, insults, imprecations, and scandal.

q: Why is suicide a sin?
a: Suicide, like murder, is a sin because God alone is the master of our life, as of our neighbor's; moreover, it is a sin of despair which, in addition, takes away with life the possibility of repenting and of being saved.

q: Has the Church established penalties against suicide?
a: The Church has established the deprivation of ecclesiastical burial against the suicide who is responsible for the act committed.

q: Why is dueling a sin?
a: Dueling is a sin because it is always an attempt at murder, and even — almost — at suicide, made out of private vengeance, in contempt of the law and of public justice; moreover, because by it the decision of right and wrong is foolishly committed to force, to skill, and to chance.

q: Has the Church established penalties against duelists?
a: The Church has established excommunication against duelists and against anyone who voluntarily attends a duel.

q: What is scandal?
a: Scandal is to give one's neighbor, by any wicked act, the occasion of sinning.

q: Is scandal a grave sin?
a: Scandal is a most grave sin, and God will demand an account of the evil that one causes others to commit by perfidious incitements and by bad example: "Woe to that man through whom scandal comes" (Matt. XVIII. 7).

q: What does the fifth commandment order us?
a: The fifth commandment orders us to wish well to all, even to our enemies, and to repair the bodily and spiritual harm done to our neighbor.

q: What does the sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not commit impure acts," forbid us?
a: The sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not commit impure acts," forbids us every impurity: therefore immoral actions, words, looks, books, images, and entertainments.

q: What does the sixth commandment order us?
a: The sixth commandment orders us to be "holy in body," showing the greatest respect for our own person and for that of others, as the works of God and as temples in which He dwells by His presence and by His grace.

q: What does the seventh commandment, "Thou shalt not steal," forbid us?
a: The seventh commandment, "Thou shalt not steal," forbids us to harm our neighbor in his goods: therefore it forbids thefts, damages, usury, frauds in contracts and in services, and lending a hand to such harms.

q: What does the seventh commandment order us?
a: The seventh commandment orders us to restore the goods of others, to repair damages culpably caused, to pay our debts, and to give the just wage to workers.

q: Will one who, being able, does not restore or repair obtain forgiveness?
a: One who, being able, does not restore or repair will not obtain forgiveness, even if in words he declares himself repentant.

q: What does the eighth commandment, "Thou shalt not bear false witness," forbid us?
a: The eighth commandment, "Thou shalt not bear false witness," forbids us every falsehood and every unjust harm to another's reputation: therefore, besides false witness, calumny, lying, detraction or murmuring, flattery, and rash judgment and suspicion.

q: What does the eighth commandment order us?
a: The eighth commandment orders us to speak the truth in due time and place, and to interpret in a good sense, when possible, the actions of our neighbor.

q: One who has harmed his neighbor in his good name by accusing him falsely or by speaking ill of him — to what is he bound?
a: One who has harmed his neighbor in his good name by accusing him falsely or by speaking ill of him must, as far as he is able, repair the harm caused.

q: What does the ninth commandment, "Thou shalt not desire thy neighbor's wife," forbid us?
a: The ninth commandment, "Thou shalt not desire thy neighbor's wife," forbids us evil thoughts and desires.

q: What does the ninth commandment order us?
a: The ninth commandment orders us perfect purity of soul, and the greatest respect — even in the depths of the heart — for the sanctuary of the family.

q: What does the tenth commandment, "Thou shalt not desire thy neighbor's goods," forbid us?
a: The tenth commandment, "Thou shalt not desire thy neighbor's goods," forbids us the unbridled greed for riches, without regard for the rights and the good of our neighbor.

q: What does the tenth commandment order us?
a: The tenth commandment orders us to be just and moderate in our desire to better our condition, and to bear with patience the hardships and other miseries permitted by the Lord for our merit, since "we must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations" (Acts XIV. 22).

q: What are the general precepts of the Church?
a: The general precepts of the Church are laws by which she, applying the commandments of God, prescribes to the faithful certain acts of religion and certain abstinences.

q: How does the Church have authority to make laws and precepts?
a: The Church has authority to make laws and precepts because she received it, in the persons of the Apostles, from Jesus Christ, the Man-God; and therefore whoever disobeys the Church disobeys God Himself.

q: In the Church, who can make laws and precepts?
a: In the Church, the Pope and the Bishops, as successors of the Apostles, can make laws and precepts; for to them Jesus Christ said: "He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me" (Luke X. 16).

q: What does the first precept, "to hear Mass on Sundays and on the other commanded feast days," order us?
a: The first precept, "to hear Mass on Sundays and on the other commanded feast days," orders us to assist devoutly at the Holy Mass on those days.

q: Is it a grave sin not to hear Mass on days of precept?
a: Whoever, without true impediment, does not hear Mass on days of precept, and whoever does not give his dependents the means to hear it, commits a grave sin and does not fulfill the divine commandment to keep the feast days holy.

q: What does the second precept forbid us by the words "do not eat meat on Friday and on the other forbidden days"?
a: The second precept, by the words "do not eat meat on Friday and on the other forbidden days," forbids us to eat meat on Fridays (the day of the Passion and Death of Jesus Christ) and on certain days of fasting. 218 a. The five general precepts of the Church: 1. To hear Mass on Sundays and on the other commanded feasts; 2. To sanctify the days of obligation; 3. To confess at least once a year and to receive Holy Communion at least at Easter; 4. To fast and abstain from meat on the appointed days; 5. To contribute to the needs of the Church according to her laws and customs.

q: What does the second precept order us by the words "to fast on the prescribed days"?
a: The second precept, by the words "to fast on the prescribed days," orders us to observe the ecclesiastical fast in Lent, on certain days of Advent, on the four Ember Days, and on certain vigils.

q: To what does the ecclesiastical fast bind us?
a: The ecclesiastical fast binds us to abstinence from certain foods, and from other meals beyond the principal one; however, a second light refection is permitted.

q: Who is bound to the ecclesiastical fast?
a: To the ecclesiastical fast every member of the faithful is bound, from the completed twenty-first year of age to the sixtieth, unless excused by infirmity, by burdensome labors, or by some other just reason.

q: Why does the Church impose abstinences and fasts on us?
a: The Church imposes abstinences and fasts on us, in conformity with the example and doctrine of Jesus Christ, for penance for our sins, for the mortification of gluttony and of the passions, and for other particular necessities.

q: What does the third precept, "to confess at least once a year and to receive Communion at least at Easter," order us?
a: The third precept, "to confess at least once a year and to receive Communion at least at Easter," orders us to approach Penance at least once a year and the Eucharist at least at Easter time.

q: Why does the Church, in commanding us to confess and receive Communion once a year, add the word "at least"?
a: The Church, in commanding us to confess and receive Communion once a year, adds the word "at least" to remind us of the usefulness, indeed the need, of receiving these sacraments often, as is her desire.

q: What does the fourth precept, "to support the necessities of the Church by contributing according to the laws or customs," order us?
a: The fourth precept, "to support the necessities of the Church by contributing according to the laws or customs," orders us to make the offerings established by authority or by usage, for the fitting exercise of worship and for the honest sustenance of the ministers of God.

q: What does the fifth precept, "not to celebrate weddings solemnly in the forbidden times," forbid?
a: The fifth precept, "not to celebrate weddings solemnly in the forbidden times," forbids the Mass with the special blessing of the spouses from the first Sunday of Advent until Holy Christmas, and from Ash Wednesday until Easter Sunday.
